dialog.body: City Clerk's office, this is Owen. How can I help you?

Oh, good morning, Owen. I hope I'm not bothering you. My name is Sofia Furtado. You know, when I was a girl we lived down near the harbor, and my father used to say the only things that came up from the water were fish and trouble. Well, now the trouble came up in my garage.
Okay. Good morning, Mrs. Furtado. Take your time. What kind of trouble is in the garage?
A raccoon. A big one. I went out this morning to get my boxes of tenant paperwork, and there he was, up on the shelf, looking at me like I was the one who didn't belong.
Oh my. A raccoon in the garage. Did it come toward you at all?
No, no. I backed out and shut the side door. But he made a noise, a kind of hissing, and I don't like it. My heart was going. I'm eighty-four, I don't move so fast anymore.
That's understandable. First, are you inside somewhere safe right now?
I'm in the kitchen of the house. The garage is the separate one, out back. I own the house, I rent out the upstairs and downstairs, so I have tenants, and I worry for them too. One has a little dog.
Alright. So the raccoon is in a detached garage, and the door is closed now. Is that right?
Yes, closed. Well, the big door has a gap at the bottom. Maybe he came in that way. I don't know.
Okay. And does the raccoon look sick at all? Stumbling, drooling, acting very confused, out in the daytime?
Well, it was daytime. About nine o'clock. He wasn't stumbling, he was sitting up there. But he did stare at me. Is that sick? Oh, I don't like that.

It could be nothing. Raccoons do move around in the daytime sometimes. I just want to get the right people out to you. Let me ask you, who is it you'd like to know about, who responds to something like this?
That's what I want to ask you. Who comes? Is it the police? The fire department? When I was little the man from the dog pound came for everything, and he had a net.

[pause] Right. Here in Newport, it's the animal control officer who handles wildlife complaints like this, and they work through the police department's dispatch. So I can pass your information along to them, or you can call it in yourself. I'd say let me take the details and get it going.
Oh, would you? That would be a relief. They'll come to the house?
They'll look at it and tell you what to do. Whether they remove it or advise you on getting it out, that depends on the situation. I can't tell you which. But someone will follow up with you.
Alright. Alright, that's fair.
I'll need an address for the garage, and a number where they can reach you.

Now here's the problem. I'm on a borrowed phone. My neighbor's grandson lent me this one because mine, the battery was dead and I couldn't find the cord. And I don't know the number of this one. I never asked him.
Okay, that's alright. Hmm. Is the neighbor close by? Could you ask them for it?
He went off to work, the grandson. His grandmother is home, but she's hard of hearing, she's got no idea about his phone either. I'm sorry, I'm a bother.
You're not a bother at all. Let's see. Sometimes the phone has a setting that shows its own number. Do you know how to look at the contacts or settings?
Oh, I'd press the wrong thing and hang up on you. I'm not good with these.
Wait. I have my own number, I know that one by heart, it's 401-555-0156. But the phone is dead, so if they call it, I won't hear it until I charge it.
Okay. 401-555-0156. I'll write that down and read it back: 401, 555, 0156. Is that right?
That's it. That's mine, my own phone. I'll plug it in as soon as I get home. Well, I am home. I'll plug it in as soon as I find the cord. It's in the car, I think.
Good. Please do that, and keep it close. Now, the address of the garage?
Oh, I'm not going to say it. Is that alright? I mean, I'd rather not on this phone line. It's a borrowed phone and all.
Hmm. Well, they will need to know where to go. Is there a reason you'd prefer not to say?

No reason, I'm just an old woman who gets nervous. [pause] Oh, never mind, listen to me. Let me think how to say it, the clerk's office is the one who can tell me what to do, and then I'll tell the officer when he calls me.

That works. I can note that you'll give the location directly to the animal control officer when they reach you. I'll flag it as a raccoon in a detached garage, possibly a daytime sighting, caller is elderly and anxious. Does that sound right?
Yes, anxious, you can put that. Worried is the word. I keep thinking, what if he gets in the house, what if the tenant's little dog goes out to the garage and gets bitten.
That's a good thing to be careful about. Until someone comes, keep the garage door shut, and ask your tenants to keep the dog on a leash and away from that building.
Yes, I'll tell them. The downstairs boy, he's good, he'll listen. I'll knock on his door right after this.
Good. And please don't try to chase it out or corner it yourself. It's better to leave it be.
Oh, no, no. I'm not about to go in there. I'd sooner call the Pope.
[pause] Fair enough. Now, a question. If it's in there and you leave the door closed, is there any food in the garage? Pet food, trash, birdseed?
Birdseed, yes. A big bag. My husband's, I mean, it's been there. And the trash barrels are by the side.
Okay. That could be what drew it. I'll add that to the note. The officer may have advice on that when they call.
Oh, the birdseed. I should have thrown that out. Well. Too late now.
It happens a lot. Nobody thinks about it.
When will they call, do you think? Today? I'd like it to be today.

I can't promise a time. It's a Thursday, late morning, so I'd hope today, but they may be out on other calls. If you haven't heard anything by the end of the afternoon, call us back, or call the police department's regular line and mention the animal control request.
The regular line. And I'll say it's about the raccoon.
Yes. Say you already made a request through the clerk's office this morning. That helps them match it up.
Alright. Let me write that down, I have a pencil here. Clerk's office, this morning, raccoon. And my own number. Oh, and what was your name again?
Owen. O-W-E-N.
Owen. Thank you, Owen. You were very patient with me. My daughter says I talk too long before I get to the point.
No, it was fine. You got there. I'll send this over right now.
Thank you. I'm going to knock on the downstairs door now. And then find that cord.
Sounds good. Take care, Mrs. Furtado.
Goodbye now.
